meta.one_idea: A call fills a function's arguments by position unless we name them. A default fills the ones we leave out. An argument is the function's own box, so changing it does not change the variable outside.
outcomes: Write a function with two arguments and call it by name, in either order.
Call it by position, and say which value lands in which argument.
Predict the output when positional values are swapped, with no error to warn you.
Read the TypeError when a call leaves an argument empty, and name the empty one.
Give an argument a default value, and predict which value each call uses.
Say why a default argument cannot come before one without a default.
Explain why increment(a) leaves a outside unchanged.

The SyntaxError text is the wording of Python 3.11 and older. Python 3.12 and newer say: parameter without a default follows parameter with a default.
The transcript shows the playground prints the old wording, so the spec keeps it. The guide tells the instructor about the new wording in case a laptop runs a newer Python.
The daily challenge calls get_list(string_a), a positional call, before slide 17 teaches positional calls. Session 22's deck had the same challenge on its slide 53.

notes: The room is 50 to 60 first-year students on laptops. Laptops stay shut except on T1, T2 and the classroom quiz, where only the worksheet tab and the playground are open.

One world for the session: Google Maps on Teja's phone, going home from the college Main Gate to Ameerpet. The hook, Task 1, the game, Hook 2 and the exit all live there. Task 2 is a Rapido fare, the ride she books on the same trip.
Concept cards keep the deck's own greet program and its inputs (Good Morning, Ram; Hello, Teja), so the room can match them to the deck in their notes later.
Words: the names in the def's brackets are arguments, as the deck says. Never say parameter. A call passes values. By name is a keyword argument; by position is a positional argument.

One picture for the whole session: An argument is drawn as a slot in the def's header. A value travels from the call into its slot. Sent by name, the value carries its label (arg_1=) and lands on the slot with that label. Sent by position, it carries its number (1st, 2nd) and lands on the slot in that place.
Votes are taken option by option: the instructor reads each option and asks how many think it is that one. Hands up. Nobody is named.
Nothing before the title card may say the session's name. The hook shows a map app, never code words like argument.
The bar to beat is Plans/DSA/Module 3 - Stacks & Queues/01 - Introduction to Stacks/: a simulation the room drives, a picture that refuses to lie.

build_contract: One self-contained HTML file. It opens offline from a USB stick and makes no network request.
It opens in presenter view. There is no sidebar, top bar or button the instructor has to use.

Right arrow or the clicker is one press. Left arrow goes back one press. F goes full screen, A shows all the cards, and End shows the whole card at once. The instructor guide tells the instructor these keys, so they must work.
Every card is its own screen, in the order of this spec. Press 1 is what shows when the card opens.
Every card's outer element carries data-spec="<card id>" and data-presses="<number of presses>". The review script reads both.
No link to any other file. The students' handout and the instructor guide are separate files, and a link from this file is how a class finds the answers.
rules: No autoplay. Nothing moves on a timer. One press, one move, with a caption that says what just happened.
Commit, then reveal. Where a card asks a question, the answer shows only on the press after the room has answered.
Wrong answers stay private. No names, no per-student results on screen. Hands are counted out loud, never shown.
The topic is named once. Nothing before the title card says today's topic, not a heading, not a caption, not a file name on a code card.

Words are exact. Words in quotation marks, and every line under Exact words, are final. The rest of a press describes what happens, in your own design. If an exact line does not fit, ask for a new one; do not rewrite it.
Code is exact. Copy code and outputs from the JSON, never retype them. Every output here came from running the program.
Simple English. Short sentences, everyday words. No em-dashes anywhere, the page title included.
Every card moves. A card that introduces an idea steps; a static card is a picture of a lecture.

cards.title: Recap: prints something, or nothing?
cards.purpose: Pull back session 22: a def alone runs nothing, a call runs the block, return hands a value back without printing it, and a line after return never runs.
cards.heading: Prints something, or nothing?
show: Five small programs from last class.
Does it print something, or nothing?
Prints something
Prints nothing

cards.title: Same name, two boxes
cards.purpose: increment(a) makes its own box named a. It changes that box to 6 and the box vanishes when the call ends, so print(a) outside shows 5.
cards.heading: Passing immutable objects
show: What will it print?
Same name, two different boxes.
Changing the value of the variable inside the function will not affect the variable outside.
Want the 6 outside? Hand it back with return.

code.src:
def increment(a):
    a += 1

a = int(input())
increment(a)
print(a)

def increment(a):
    a += 1
    return a

a = int(input())
a = increment(a)
print(a)

presses.screen: One move per press, following data.steps, caption from the data. Outside, a box a holds 5. The call opens increment's area with its own box a holding 5. a += 1 changes that inside box to 6. The call ends: the inside box and its 6 vanish. print(a) reads the outside box.
presses.say: Which a is Python looking at now?

presses.screen: Deck slide 45 and 47's picture: the outside box 5 ringed, the output <q>5</q>. Caption: <q>Same name, two different boxes.</q> then <q>Changing the value of the variable inside the function will not affect the variable outside.</q>
presses.say: Numbers and strings are immutable: a += 1 makes a new 6 for the inside box. The outside 5 is untouched.

presses.screen: increment_return.py: line 3 return a, line 6 a = increment(a). It prints <q>6</q>. Caption: <q>Want the 6 outside? Hand it back with return.</q>

The two boxes both read a. Their places (inside the function, outside) tell them apart.

increment is done. Its box is gone. Python jumps back to line 5.
